tldr: By extracting the hitting and serving forms of Nadal, Federer, and Djokovic from broadcast tennis match videos, this study proposes AdaPT, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework equipped with a speed adaptation mechanism, achieving both professional stylistic motion and high hitting success rates on real whole-body humanoid robots.
hero_caption: Overall framework of AdaPT. (a) Motion data is constructed from broadcast videos via pose estimation, retargeting, and physics refinement. (b) A low-level tracking policy robust to varying execution speeds is trained. (c) A high-level planner autonomously adjusts the execution speed along with the motion latent variable. (d) This enables zero-shot deployment to the real Unitree G1 and full-size humanoid robot Atom.
overview:
In recent years, humanoid robots have achieved growing success in ball sports. However, most prior work focuses solely on making contact and returning the ball, failing to reproduce the refined motion styles displayed by elite human athletes. From a sports biomechanics perspective, an elite athlete's form is not just visually appealing; it is an exceptionally rational coordinated movement that generates maximum force under limited muscle and actuator capacity while quickly recovering back to a ready stance.

To address this, the authors developed AdaPT, an integrated framework that extracts motion styles from broadcast tennis matches and enables humanoids to learn both rallies and serves. To return balls without degrading style, AdaPT adopts a decoupled motion planning and tracking architecture that separates a high-level planner generating kinematic trajectories from a low-level tracker controlling joint torques. However, deploying this architecture directly to real robots exposes a severe sim-to-real gap, where actuator discrepancies, perception noise, and compounding autoregressive planning drift cascade, leading to frequent misses in the real world.

The key solution is explicit Speed Adaptation. The low-level tracker learns to track references at randomized execution speeds for robustness, while the high-level planner is given the flexibility to adjust the progression speed of the motion based on the situation. In real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 and Dobot Atom, the robot maintained the distinct styles of Nadal, Federer, and Djokovic while achieving high return and serve success rates, and demonstrated serve deployment using camera vision in environments without motion capture.
contributions: Built an end-to-end data pipeline that automatically extracts rally and serve motions with attribute labels from broadcast tennis match videos and applies physics refinement for humanoid robots.

Substantially bridged the sim-to-real gap inherent to decoupled planning-and-tracking architectures by combining randomized speed training in the low-level tracker with dynamic execution speed control in the high-level planner.

Successfully deployed rallies and serves on real hardware, including the Unitree G1 and the full-size Dobot Atom humanoid (approx. 1.7 m tall), while faithfully preserving the styles of three elite professionals.
Demonstrated in-the-wild serves without motion capture using camera vision (YOLO + stereo triangulation) and VIVE trackers, paving the way for practical applications.

sections.heading: Why Do Humanoid Robots Need the Form of Professional Tennis Players?
sections.summary: Conventional robotic ball sports have prioritized hitting success over motion style. However, professional form is essential for efficient force generation and rapid recovery, and this work proposes AdaPT to transfer rally and serve styles directly from professional match footage to real robots.
sections.details:
Tennis is an exceptionally challenging sport involving diverse strokes—forehands, backhands, slices, and topspins—along with high-speed footwork and precise whole-body coordination. Existing robotic studies in table tennis and badminton often treat simply returning the ball as the sole objective. Yet, the fluid motion of elite athletes embodies practical biomechanical wisdom: it harnesses the kinetic chain of the entire body to maximize racket head speed with minimal effort and quickly regains balance after impact. For humanoid robots with strict torque and velocity limits on actuators, learning these professional styles offers immense value.

In this study, motions of Rafael Nadal, Roger Federer, and Novak Djokovic were extracted from YouTube match broadcasts. The authors designed a hierarchical framework that preserves stylistic strokes while adapting to varying incoming balls. It uses a decoupled design where a high-level planner generates the kinematic motion backbone and a low-level tracker executes it. A motion generator (MVAE) planning approach is adopted for rallies, while residual tracking is used for serves.

However, directly transferring this decoupled design to real hardware induces a large sim-to-real gap: actuator response delays, compounding autoregressive model drift, and camera perception noise accumulate, causing motions that succeeded in simulation to fail on real robots. To resolve this, the framework introduces speed adaptation by randomizing tracking speeds during policy training and empowering the planner to dynamically modulate the progression speed of the motion.

sections.heading: What Was Missing in Prior Ball-Sports Robots and Imitation Learning?
sections.summary: Many previous studies tightly coupled environmental dynamics with motion priors, sacrificing professional form for hitting performance. Decoupled approaches, on the other hand, suffered from compounding errors on real hardware, and this work bridges both challenges through speed adaptation.
sections.details:
Robotic ball sports have a long research history, and recent reinforcement learning advances have shown remarkable progress in soccer, basketball, table tennis, and tennis. However, most focus solely on task success (hit rate). Reproducing dynamic whole-body styles—especially serving, which requires tossing the ball and utilizing full-body whip-like coordination—remains largely unexplored on real humanoid hardware.

Among motion learning approaches, methods like PULSE and LATENT tightly couple a motion prior with environment interaction. While achieving high hit rates, they tend to severely distort the motion style when reacting to the ball, resulting in unnatural footwork and awkward swings.

Conversely, approaches like Vid2Player3D completely decouple motion planning from joint tracking, which helps maintain stylistic fidelity. However, when real-world actuator discrepancies and vision sensor latency/noise feed back into the planner, errors snowball autoregressively, leading to frequent misses on the real robot. AdaPT builds upon this decoupled architecture while incorporating a speed adaptation mechanism to achieve both style preservation and real-world task robustness.

sections.heading: Adaptive Planning and Tracking: AdaPT's Architecture and Learning Mechanisms
sections.summary: High-quality tennis motion data was extracted from match videos, and distinct hierarchical pipelines were constructed for the fundamentally different tasks of rallying and serving. The low-level speed-adaptive tracker and high-level speed-modulating planner work together to flexibly handle real-world discrepancies.
sections.details:
Rallying requires reactive diversity in response to opponent shots, whereas serving demands high repeatability and precision to toss and strike one's own ball. Focusing on this difference, the framework implements specialized strategies for each task.

3.1 Motion Data Construction
Human 3D poses are reconstructed from broadcast videos using GVHMR and retargeted to the humanoid skeleton with GMR. After correcting video-specific wrist occlusions, a generalized tracker runs in a physics simulator to refine the motions into dynamically feasible joint trajectories. Each motion is annotated with player identity, stroke type (forehand/backhand), spin type (topspin/slice), and impact timing.

3.2 Speed-Adaptive Motion Tracker
The low-level tracker converts a target pose $\hat{\bm{q}}_t$ into PD control setpoints. Crucially, it blends the previous and current frames with a factor $\alpha \in [\alpha_{\mathrm{min}}, \alpha_{\mathrm{max}}]$ via $\hat{\bm{q}}_t^\alpha = (1-\alpha)\hat{\bm{q}}_{t-1} + \alpha\hat{\bm{q}}_t$. Randomizing $\alpha$ during training enables the tracker to robustly execute motions whether they advance faster or slower than normal.

3.3 High-Level Planning with Speed Adaptation
- Rally Learning: Built upon Vid2Player3D, an MVAE autoregressively generates the next pose from a latent code $\bm{z}_t$. The high-level planner $\pi^{\mathrm{rally}}_{\mathrm{plan}}$ receives predicted future ball trajectories and outputs both the latent code $\bm{z}_t$ and the tracker's execution speed $\alpha_t$. This allows the robot to accelerate its swing if the ball arrives faster than expected, or hold back if the ball is slower.
- Serve Learning: Given the lower behavioral diversity in serves, residual tracking is adopted instead of an MVAE, outputting residual actions $\Delta\bm{a}_t$ over reference motions. Because pure hit rewards encourage the policy to bypass the backswing (local optimum), the frame with the deepest racket drop is designated as a keyframe, scaling the local tracking reward weight by $50\times$ to enforce proper form.
- Toss Control and Domain Randomization: The toss is guided by a parabolic ballistic model reward. Adding noise to gripper release timing and initial velocity accommodates physical hand friction and actuator delays on the real robot.

sections.heading: Replicating Pro Techniques on the Real Unitree G1: Experiments and In-Depth Analysis
sections.summary: Real-world tennis court experiments with the Unitree G1 demonstrated high rally return rates and accurate serves while preserving the distinct forms of Nadal, Federer, and Djokovic. Ablation studies highlighted the critical roles of speed adaptation, future trajectory prediction, and toss guidance.
sections.details:
4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on a scaled tennis court (Tennis 10s standard: $18\times 6.5\mathrm{m}$) inside an approximately $20\mathrm{m}\times 8\mathrm{m}$ arena equipped with 35 motion capture cameras. The robot was a 1.35 m tall Unitree G1 equipped with a 23-inch junior racket mounted at a 25-degree wrist offset. For rally evaluations, a ball machine (Acemate) delivered balls along unseen trajectories with 25 trials per condition.

4.2 Simulation Analysis
Training reinforcement learning from scratch (RL-Scratch) yielded high hit rates but terrible style fidelity ($E_{\mathrm{FID}}$), resulting in unnatural motions. Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) tracked rally contacts but degraded footwork, and failed in serves by missing phase-structured force generation. AdaPT achieved both high hit rates and low FID scores across all three professional styles.

4.3 Real-World Validation and Sim-to-Real
In real-world rallies, Vid2Player3D without adaptation suffered a steep decline in over-the-net success. In contrast, AdaPT, which combines an adaptive tracker (suppressing low-level tracking error) and an adaptive planner (modulating high-level timing), recorded the highest over-the-net rates and stable shots on both forehands and backhands. In serves, speed adaptation absorbed toss variations, consistently delivering successful serves with deep backswings and powerful forearm pronation.

4.4 Analysis of Key Components
- Future Trajectory Horizon: In decoupled architectures, providing multi-step future ball predictions drastically improves hitting performance. In contrast, tightly coupled methods like PULSE react quickly and can operate with shorter horizons, but at the expense of motion fidelity.
- Value of Toss Guidance: Without toss guidance rewards, the robot prioritized hitting ease by tossing extremely low, leaving insufficient time to accelerate the racket and losing landing accuracy.

4.5 Sources of the Sim-to-Real Gap
Prediction errors in post-bounce ball trajectories were identified as the most fatal factor hurting rally success, while camera estimation noise (YOLO + stereo triangulation) was the primary cause of overall performance drops.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Challenges for Humanoid Ball Sports
sections.summary: AdaPT successfully transferred professional tennis styles to humanoids while ensuring robust real-world execution. Looking ahead, improvements are needed in whole-body locomotion range, full vision-based autonomy, and wrist actuation performance.
sections.details:
This work presented AdaPT, a comprehensive framework that goes beyond merely hitting tennis balls to faithfully reproducing the refined motion styles of professional athletes on humanoid robots. The philosophy of decoupling planning from tracking and introducing dual-level speed adaptation provides valuable guidance for future whole-body dynamic motion learning.

However, several clear limitations remain. First, robot and ball state tracking still largely depend on external motion capture systems. Although serve experiments using camera vision alone proved successful, sustaining fast rallies requires a lower-latency, more robust tracking pipeline. Second, there is a trade-off between style fidelity and real-time agility: strictly enforcing aesthetic form limits wide-range locomotion toward distant incoming balls. Third, hardware constraints—particularly wrist actuator torque limits and backlash—hinder fine-grained racket face orientation control, calling for further advances in robotic hardware.

sections.heading: Appendix: Behind the Scenes of Real-World Implementation and Additional Experiments
sections.summary: The appendix details hardware and algorithmic implementation choices, including MVAE state design, reward formulations, YOLO-based 3D ball tracking from cameras, and in-the-wild serves on the full-size robot Atom.
sections.details:
The appendix reveals practical engineering and algorithmic details not fully covered in the main text.

- Vision-Based Ball Tracking Pipeline: In real-world deployment, conventional HSV color segmentation with ROI filtering was vulnerable to ambient lighting changes. The authors instead adopted YOLO detection paired with multi-camera stereo triangulation across six cameras. Confidence-weighted fusion based on camera-to-ball distance is filtered through an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate smooth 3D position and velocity.

- System Identification: Using data from 20 real ball bounces on the court, the coefficient of restitution and horizontal drag parameters were optimized and integrated into the simulation physics parameters.

- Locomotion Limitations: While autoregressive motion generation via MVAE produces rhythmic and graceful tennis forms, it restricts aggressive long-distance sprint-and-reach movements (hit success drops significantly as ball landing locations deviate from the home position).

- Multi-Fingered Hand Serving and Outdoor Deployment: When serving with the Unitree Dex-3 three-fingered hand, its heavy weight risked balance loss during high-speed professional swings; switching to an amateur-style swing with reduced arm velocity achieved a 90% (9/10) success rate. Furthermore, by pairing HTC VIVE trackers with cameras, autonomous serves were demonstrated on the full-size Dobot Atom humanoid (approx. 1.7 m tall) in outdoor environments without motion capture cameras.

captions.F12: Heatmap of hitting success rate across ball landing locations on the court (horizontal axis $y$, vertical axis $x$). Toward the sidelines far from the robot's base stance (large $y$), success drops because prioritizing style preservation impedes reaching distant balls in time.

takeaways: Style fidelity and reactive agility easily trade off against each other, but decoupling planning from tracking and adaptively modulating execution speed at both levels achieves high performance in both dimensions on real hardware.

When trained purely on hitting rewards, reinforcement learning policies exploit shortcuts like eliminating backswings or tossing unnaturally low; incorporating keyframe tracking rewards and toss guidance is essential to preserve power and landing accuracy.
Deploying decoupled architectures to real hardware heavily hinges on future trajectory prediction accuracy (especially post-bounce) and mitigating autoregressive drift.
limitations: Heavy reliance on an autoregressive MVAE restricts wide-area locomotion, such as rapidly sprinting to return balls aimed far away from the robot's base position.
Fully autonomous rallying still relies on external motion capture systems, as multi-camera real-time visual tracking faces ongoing latency and precision hurdles.
Actuator compliance and torque limits in the wrists and arms prevent maintaining balance during high-velocity full-swing serves when equipped with heavy multi-fingered hands.
